newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-GLORY YEARS AHEAD FOR REMARKABLE HINGIS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GLORY YEARS AHEAD FOR REMARKABLE HINGIS.

text.p: Martina Hingis skipped down the Wimbledon trail blazed by her great namesake Martina Navratilova on Saturday, treating her success like a latter-day Swiss fairy-tale.

The 16-year-old's achievement in becoming the youngest Wimbledon singles champion this century provided further proof the women's game has entered a new era, but Hingis herself remains refreshingly unfazed by all the attention.

"It might be that I'm maybe too young to win this title," she admitted, struggling to describe the emotions she felt on receiving the trophy from the Duchess of Kent after her 2-6 6-3 6-3 victory over Jana Novotna.
"Maybe tomorrow I will realise I won this tournament. It feels great, it's like a dream come true."

Hingis has already claimed a Wimbledon doubles title as a 15-year-old last year and, as she hurried off to play in the mixed doubles with South African partner John-Laffnie De Jager, Navratilova's awesome tally of 19 titles at the All England Club suddenly began to appear less daunting.
Novotna, beaten again after leading in the third set of a Wimbledon final, is among those convinced the smiling Swiss teenager will be the player to beat for many years to come.
"Even though Martina is very young, I have a lot of respect for her," Novotna said. "She is very professional, she is very talented and very respectful for other players."
"She's also a very nice person who enjoys her success. I think she will be very good because I think she is very normal, compared to other people who have burned out early."

Novotna revealed the two finalists had spent the morning chatting together in the trainer's room, in marked contrast to the chilly atmosphere which surrounded her last final appearance against Steffi Graf.
Hingis, who also collected the Australian Open title in January, even good-humouredly allowed her disappointed opponent to steal the winner's engraved plate and offered a generous tribute afterwards.

"She deserves to win one of the Grand Slam titles, and on this surface she's really hard. But I was the luckier one today," said Hingis, her straight sets final defeat to Iva Majoli at Roland Garros looking even more of a blip on her otherwise unbeaten record this year.

"I knew I wasn't in great shape at the French Open, but this time I knew I could do it. It was a really good chance for me. I was seeded number one and all the players in my half of the draw lost. I didn't even have to beat a seeded player to reach the final."
Engagingly, Hingis admitted she had copied her lone post-victory lap of honour from watching Graf on television.
"I watched her do it a couple of times, so I was just trying to do the same thing. All the people stood up and I almost felt like crying because it really happened to me."
Graf, Monica Seles and all the current top players should be the ones shedding the tears, because a fully fit Hingis looks set to reign well into the next century.
Even Virginia Wade, the ex-British champion who won the same title 20 years ago this week, conceded that Hingis is already setting new standards.
"She has inordinate ability and a smart tennis brain," said Wade. "She's up there in all departments."
